item.title: TuxBot, Gemini CLI Abuse, OpenClaw Flaws, and Zoom CVE-2026-53412
item.content:encoded:
Zoom warns of critical account takeover vulnerability — Must Read

Zoom patched a critical Windows flaw, CVE-2026-53412, that could let unauthenticated attackers take over accounts via network access. Users should update Zoom Workplace, VDI Client, and Meeting SDK for Windows immediately.

  • Zoom warned of a critical improper input validation vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412, in its desktop client and software development kit for Windows.
  • CVE-2026-53412 has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and may allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an account takeover via network access.
  • The flaw affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.0.0, the Windows VDI Client before versions 7.0.10, 6.6.15, and 6.5.18, and the Meeting SDK for Windows before version 7.0.0.
  • Zoom recommends that users apply the latest updates to mitigate the risks from CVE-2026-53412.
  • Zoom’s latest security patches also address three high-severity Windows-related flaws tracked as CVE-2026-53410, CVE-2026-53409, and CVE-2026-53411, and there are no indications at disclosure that any fixed vulnerabilities are being exploited.

Four New OpenClaw Vulnerabilities: When AI Agents Become the Attacker's Execution Layer — Should Read

Cyera researchers disclosed four OpenClaw vulnerabilities that can let attackers use an AI agent’s own privileges to escape filesystem sandboxes, leak secrets, escalate to owner-level control, and gain persistence. The key takeaway is that agentic AI platforms must be treated as high-privilege execution environments requiring strong isolation, identity enforcement, and runtime controls.

  • Cyera researchers discovered four OpenClaw vulnerabilities affecting filesystem isolation, privilege escalation, and data exposure.
  • CVE-2026-44112 is a critical TOCTOU filesystem write escape that can redirect writes outside the sandbox boundary and allow attackers to overwrite sensitive files, modify configurations, plant malicious scripts, or create persistence mechanisms.
  • CVE-2026-44118 is a high-severity MCP loopback privilege escalation flaw where OpenClaw trusts a client-controlled ownership flag, allowing an authenticated local child process to elevate to owner-level privileges.
  • CVE-2026-44115 can expose sensitive environment variables such as API keys or credentials through variable expansion inside unquoted heredocs despite command allowlist validation.
  • Cyera says Shodan shows more than 65,000 and Zoomeye shows more than 180,000 publicly accessible OpenClaw instances as of May 2026.

TuxBot v3 Evolution Shows Signs of LLM-Assisted IoT Botnet Development — Should Read

Researchers uncovered TuxBot v3 Evolution, an IoT botnet framework that appears to have been partly built with LLM assistance, including leftover AI-generated comments and flawed code. Despite bugs, it shows how AI can help a single developer assemble a more ambitious botnet with encrypted C2, fallback channels, DDoS features, and IoT exploitation capabilities.

  • Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 disclosed a previously unreported IoT botnet framework called TuxBot v3 Evolution that shows signs of being developed with large language model assistance.
  • Unit 42 said the analyzed samples contained leftover AI safety disclaimers and raw LLM chain-of-thought reasoning in comments, while several functions failed to work correctly.
  • TuxBot v3 Evolution includes a C-based bot agent, a Go-based command-and-control server with a DDoS-for-hire panel, a custom exploit virtual machine, Docker-based test infrastructure, and an automated build system.
  • The bot agent is designed to brute-force Telnet access using 1,496 credential pairs and includes exploit code targeting more than 30 IoT device families with known vulnerabilities.
  • Unit 42 said shared infrastructure with Kaitori v3.9 and AISURU tooling places the TuxBot operator within the Keksec ecosystem, which is known for running multiple IoT botnet variants in parallel.

Google Gemini CLI abused as a hacking agent, malware botnet operator — Should Read

A Russian-speaking threat actor used Google’s Gemini CLI as an AI hacking agent to migrate and operate a small botnet controlling systems at a dental clinic, with the tool generating code, deploying infrastructure, troubleshooting issues, and managing infected machines through natural-language prompts.

  • A Russian-speaking threat actor known as “bandcampro” used Google’s open-source Gemini CLI AI tool as a hacking agent and to operate a small-scale botnet.
  • Trend Micro researchers said the threat actor used Gemini CLI to migrate the botnet to a new command-and-control infrastructure, including architecture, coding, VPS deployment, Cloudflare configuration, and debugging in six minutes.
  • The botnet controlled eight systems in a dental clinic, and the threat actor used the AI tool to try to access the OpenDental database.
  • Daily operation logs showed the threat actor managed the botnet through natural-language requests, including asking which machines were online, listing files, and generating infection links.
  • Trend Micro said the botnet was lightweight and unsophisticated, using three plain-text files, an in-memory Python HTTP server, PowerShell agents, and persistence through scheduled tasks, WMI events, and registry modifications.

Dutch police bust investment fraud ring stealing over €100 million — Should Read

Dutch police arrested multiple suspects tied to a major international investment fraud ring that allegedly ran 20 call centers with over 700 fake financial advisers and may have stolen more than €100 million per month. Authorities say tens of thousands of victims were lured into fake investment platforms and persuaded to send cryptocurrency while being shown fictitious profits.

  • Dutch Police arrested multiple individuals suspected of involvement in an international investment fraud scheme with tens of thousands of victims.
  • Authorities believe the group operated 20 call centers with more than 700 people posing as financial advisers and at one point generated more than €100 million per month.
  • The main suspect, a 46-year-old Israeli-Polish national, was arrested in Poland on May 26, extradited to the Netherlands, and placed in detention pending trial.
  • The fraudsters built trust with victims, directed them to realistic-looking investment platforms showing fictitious profits, and persuaded them to increase investments through cryptocurrency transfers.
  • Dutch authorities linked at least 550 fraud reports and $28.6 million in reported losses to the organization, while estimating that many victims worldwide lost more than €10,000 each.

Trump administration unveils AI-supported clearinghouse for cyber vulnerabilities — Should Read

The Trump administration launched Gold Eagle, a Treasury-housed federal clearinghouse that uses AI to help government, industry, and critical infrastructure operators find, validate, prioritize, and patch cyber vulnerabilities faster. Officials said the effort depends on reauthorization of the CISA 2015 Act, which expires in September.

  • The Trump administration announced Gold Eagle, an already operative federal clearinghouse that uses artificial intelligence to help industry, critical infrastructure operators, and government detect, prioritize, and patch cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
  • Gold Eagle is housed in the Treasury Department with support from the Pentagon, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and open-source software providers are also participating.
  • A senior White House official said the clearinghouse is ingesting and validating vulnerabilities and that administrators are creating a system to distribute vulnerabilities to stakeholders without risking leaks.
  • Closed source models including Anthropic’s Mythos will be used in the vulnerability-hunting effort, according to the official.
  • Officials said Gold Eagle is made possible by the CISA 2015 Act and that the effort would be fundamentally challenged if Congress does not reauthorize the law before it expires in September.

Enrichment Shouldn't Cost You a Lookup: Introducing Censys Unlimited Enrichment — Optional

Censys launched Unlimited Enrichment, a credit-free host enrichment API designed to let security teams enrich every external IP in SIEM, SOAR, and AI SOC workflows without rationing lookups. The key takeaway is that Censys wants IP context to become an always-on first step in alert triage rather than a costly, selective investigation step.

  • Censys introduced Unlimited Enrichment, a credit-free host enrichment API for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
  • Unlimited Enrichment returns a compact, standardized profile that includes geolocation, network and ASN ownership, DNS data, open ports and protocols, labels, Censys ARC Reputation Score, detected threats, and third-party context.
  • Censys designed the API for high-volume automated lookups in SIEM, SOAR, and AI SOC pipelines so teams can enrich alerts at the start of triage instead of rationing lookups.
  • The article describes example uses for firewall, EDR, DLP, and IAM alerts where enrichment data can help analysts decide whether to close, escalate, contain, or investigate further.
  • Unlimited Enrichment is available as an option on the Censys Core plan.

item.title: SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days, AsyncAPI npm Compromise, and ClaudeFix MacSync Stealer
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-15409, CVE-2026-15410: SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-day vulnerabilities exploited in the wild — Must Read

SonicWall patched two actively exploited SMA 1000 zero-day vulnerabilities that could be chained for unauthenticated remote code execution on internet-facing appliances. Organizations should urgently upgrade to the fixed versions and review SonicWall’s indicators of compromise for signs of exploitation.

  • SonicWall disclosed and patched CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, two zero-day vulnerabilities in SMA 1000 Series secure remote access appliances that have been exploited in the wild.
  • CVE-2026-15409 is a server-side request forgery flaw in the SMA 1000 Workplace interface, and CVE-2026-15410 is a code injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console.
  • The article says the two flaws may be chained together to allow fully remote, unauthenticated arbitrary OS command execution on affected appliances.
  • CISA added both CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog with a remediation date of July 17.
  • SonicWall released fixed versions for affected SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v, and its advisory includes indicators of compromise for threat hunters.

AsyncAPI npm packages infected with credential-stealing malware — Must Read

Attackers compromised AsyncAPI GitHub Actions workflows to publish five malicious npm package versions that delivered a credential-stealing remote access trojan, affecting packages with over 2.25 million weekly downloads. The malicious versions have been removed, but developers should check lock files and existing installs, remove payloads, kill suspicious processes, and rotate credentials on affected systems.

  • Five malicious versions of AsyncAPI npm packages were published in a supply-chain attack after a threat actor exploited a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow.
  • The trojanized packages in the @asyncapi namespace had a cumulative weekly download count of more than 2.25 million.
  • Researchers said the attack used the repositories’ legitimate release workflows and npm’s GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration, resulting in packages with legitimate SLSA provenance attestations.
  • The malware retrieved additional payloads from IPFS, established persistence, and communicated with command-and-control infrastructure over HTTP, Nostr relays, Ethereum smart contracts, and a libp2p mesh network.
  • All five malicious package versions have been removed from npm, but developers are advised to check existing installations and lock files, remove the hidden NodeJS/sync.js payload, terminate malicious processes, and rotate credentials on impacted systems.

OkoBot Malware Framework Injects Seed Phrase Phishing Into Ledger and Trezor Apps — Must Read

OkoBot is a Windows malware framework that injects fake seed-phrase recovery pages directly into legitimate Ledger and Trezor desktop apps, sometimes waiting for a real device to be connected before phishing the user. The wallets themselves are not broken; the compromise is on the endpoint, so users should treat any desktop prompt asking for a recovery phrase as malicious unless it is explicitly required on the hardware device screen.

  • Kaspersky's GReAT team reported that the OkoBot malware framework has been active on Windows machines since April 2025 and counted hundreds of victims across more than 25 countries.
  • OkoBot's SeedHunter module injects into Trezor Suite, Ledger Wallet, and Ledger Live, hooks the Electron internals, and displays a fake recovery phrase page inside the legitimate wallet application.
  • SeedHunter can wait until a real Ledger or Trezor device is plugged in before showing its malicious recovery page, then sends the typed phrase to its command-and-control server.
  • Kaspersky identified ClickFix lures and trojanized GitHub software as two main infection paths, including a repository that advertised SQL Server Management Studio but shipped a maliciously modified Audacity build.
  • The OkoBot toolkit also includes surveillance and theft components that collect wallet files, cookies, browser profiles, credentials, keystrokes, screenshots, and recordings of selected application windows.

ClaudeFix: Shared Claude Chats Meet ClickFix — Should Read

Zscaler found a MacSync Stealer campaign that used Google malvertising to send Mac users searching for Claude to shared Claude chats containing ClickFix paste-and-run commands. The commands launched a multi-stage macOS infection chain that stole credentials, files, and cryptocurrency wallet data while abusing trusted AI platform features for legitimacy.

  • Zscaler Threat Hunting identified a ClickFix campaign that abused Anthropic’s Claude platform by using shared Claude chats to host commands that led to MacSync Stealer infections.
  • The campaign used paid Google ads to lure Mac users searching for terms such as “claude download” into shared Claude chats that appeared more legitimate because they were hosted on the official Claude domain.
  • Victims were instructed to run a curl command with a Base64-obfuscated URL, which launched a multi-stage macOS infection chain using zsh and osascript.
  • MacSync Stealer can steal keychain files, browser credentials and cookies, sensitive files, Telegram data, shell history, cloud keys, and cryptocurrency wallet data from affected systems.
  • Zscaler observed the malvertising campaign running from June 12–19, 2026, and noted Russian-language comments in the third-stage AppleScript payload.

23andMe reaches $18 million settlement with states for massive breach — Should Read

23andMe agreed to an $18 million settlement with 42 state attorneys general over cybersecurity failures tied to its 2023 breach that exposed data on 6.9 million people, including genetic ancestry information. The deal also imposes new security oversight and preserves customers’ rights to delete personal data and destroy genetic samples.

  • A coalition of 42 state attorneys general reached an $18 million settlement with 23andMe over cybersecurity failings tied to a breach that exposed information on 6.9 million people, including genetic ancestry data.
  • The settlement requires new data protection measures from the 23andMe Research Institute, including risk assessments and a special board to oversee data security.
  • The settlement requires that 23andMe customers continue to have the right to destroy their genetic samples and delete personal data indefinitely.
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James’ office said 23andMe lacked protections against hacks using stolen credentials, had insufficient intrusion prevention, failed to log or monitor breaches, and did not fix known vulnerabilities.
  • The 23andMe Research Institute bought 23andMe’s assets in July 2025, including genetic data for customers who had not requested that their information be destroyed.

Dutch police dismantle global crypto investment scam, arrest alleged mastermind — Should Read

Dutch police dismantled a global fake cryptocurrency investment network that allegedly used call centers and bogus trading platforms to steal more than €100 million a month from tens of thousands of victims. The alleged mastermind, described as a well-known hacker with Israeli and Polish citizenship, was arrested and extradited to the Netherlands.

  • Dutch police dismantled an international investment fraud network that allegedly tricked tens of thousands of people into investing in fake cryptocurrency schemes.
  • Authorities said the group had operated since at least 2021, running about two dozen call centers across several countries and employing more than 700 people posing as professional financial advisers.
  • Police said the operation generated more than €100 million per month by persuading victims to invest through bogus trading platforms after building relationships with them by phone and online.
  • A 46-year-old man with Israeli and Polish citizenship, described by Dutch police as a well-known hacker, was arrested in May at a Polish airport after arriving from Dubai and extradited to the Netherlands.
  • Dutch police estimate that victims in the Netherlands alone lost nearly €25 million, and they said many victims did not know they had been scammed until investigators contacted them.

We built a vulnerability vending machine: AI tokens in, zero-days out — Should Read

Intruder says it built an AI-assisted vulnerability research pipeline that uses code slicing and LLMs to find and exploit real bugs, including a blind SQL injection zero-day in the Creative Mail WordPress plugin affecting sites that also run WooCommerce. The key takeaway is that current AI models, when given focused code context, can already automate meaningful vulnerability discovery and exploit development.

  • Intruder built a pipeline that uses Joern to scan codebases, generate focused program slices, and pass relevant context to LLMs for triage, exploitability assessment, and exploit development.
  • The pipeline was tested against the top 200 WordPress plugins, with an emphasis on unauthenticated attack surface such as REST routes, template hooks, and nopriv AJAX calls.
  • The first vulnerability found by the pipeline was CVE-2026-3985, a blind SQL injection in the Creative Mail WordPress plugin that requires WooCommerce to be installed alongside it.
  • Intruder says the exploitation agent produced a working proof of concept capable of confirming the issue and extracting password hashes from the database.
  • The Creative Mail plugin has been pulled from the WordPress store pending review, and the article advises users running Creative Mail with WooCommerce to disable it until a patch is available.

Understanding Claude Tag’s access model in Slack and how to configure it securely — May Read

Claude Tag in Slack uses admin-configured shared access bundles rather than the credentials of the user who tags it, making channel membership and bundle scope part of the access-control boundary. Organizations should keep bundles least-privileged, restrict sensitive bundles to private channels, and use Claude Enterprise login/RBAC controls to limit who can direct the agent.

  • Claude Tag acts on connected services in shared Slack channels using admin-configured shared credentials, not the credentials of the user who tags it.
  • Access bundles group connector credentials and can be attached to a workspace or specific channel, allowing channel members to direct Claude within the scope configured by an administrator.
  • Organizations can require claude.ai login and role-based access control so that only qualifying users can start Claude sessions or interact with Claude in existing threads.
  • The article recommends auditing access bundles, reviewing channel membership and bundle scope together, using minimum-privilege bundles, and managing channel invite policies for sensitive channels.
  • Tenable Research worked with Anthropic’s security team through coordinated disclosure, and Anthropic said feedback about the admin configuration experience was shared with the relevant product team.

There and Back Again: An Operators Guide on NTLM Relaying Egress — May Read

SpecterOps describes a practical NTLM relay technique that coerces SMB or WebDAV authentication out to an internet-facing cloud host, tunnels it back through red team infrastructure, and relays it into the target network to achieve privilege escalation. The key defense is enforcing LDAP signing/LDAPS channel binding, enabling EPA on ADCS web enrollment, and restricting outbound SMB and unnecessary inbound traffic.

  • SpecterOps describes “There and Back Again” as a technique that coerces outbound NTLM authentication to an internet-facing cloud host, forwards it back to red team infrastructure, and proxies it into the target environment to relay to services such as ADCS web enrollment or LDAP/LDAPS.
  • The technique is useful when operators only have low-privilege command-and-control access and cannot bind locally to port 445/TCP or when firewall rules prevent more traditional WebDAV relays inside the environment.
  • The article states that vulnerable ADCS web enrollment endpoints lacking Extended Protection for Authentication are still seen in nearly 70–80% of client environments with an Active Directory presence.
  • The article demonstrates a local privilege escalation flow using WebDAV coercion over port 443/TCP, DNS record creation, EFS and WebClient service preparation, ntlmrelayx relay to LDAPS, shadow credentials, Certipy authentication, S4U2Self, and WMI execution.
  • The defensive guidance recommends enabling LDAP signing and LDAPS channel binding, enabling Extended Protection for Authentication on ADCS web enrollment endpoints, restricting outbound SMB to public IPs, and deploying local firewall rules that allow only necessary inbound ports.

A Trivia Game at Black Hat Asia & the Case for Network Visibility | Corelight — Optional

Corelight used a trivia game at Black Hat Asia to illustrate why strong network visibility is essential for detecting threats and understanding what is happening across an environment.

  • The article is a Corelight piece titled “A Trivia Game at Black Hat Asia & the Case for Network Visibility.”
  • The article discusses a trivia game at Black Hat Asia.
  • The article connects the trivia game to a case for network visibility.

item.title: Microsoft 622-CVE Patch Tuesday: Exploited SharePoint, ADFS Flaws and Critical Browser Updates
item.content:encoded:
Researcher Drops New Windows Zero-Day PoC Hours After Microsoft Patch Tuesday — Must Read

A researcher released a PoC for LegacyHive, a Windows User Profile Service privilege escalation zero-day that reportedly works on fully patched Windows systems after July 2026 Patch Tuesday. The disclosure comes amid Microsoft’s record patch release and active exploitation of several SharePoint Server and ADFS vulnerabilities now tracked by CISA.

  • Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as Nightmare-Eclipse, released a proof-of-concept exploit called LegacyHive for a Windows User Profile Service arbitrary hive load elevation of privileges vulnerability.
  • The LegacyHive proof of concept reportedly works on all supported desktop and server versions of Windows, including systems with the latest July 2026 Patch Tuesday update.
  • Chaotic Eclipse said the public proof of concept was stripped down to prevent public exploitation and that the original exploit did not require additional user credentials or limit loading to the usrclass.dat hive.
  • Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixed a record 622 flaws, including actively exploited privilege escalation vulnerabilities in SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-56164 and CVE-2026-56155 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and said it is aware of active exploitation of multiple SharePoint Server flaws affecting supported on-premises SharePoint Server versions.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-56164) SharePoint Server Privilege Escalation via Missing Authentication — Must Read

CVE-2026-56164 is a zero-day privilege escalation flaw in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server that has been exploited in the wild, so internet-facing farms should be patched through SharePoint’s own update process immediately. Organizations should also verify exposure, review logs for compromise, and prioritize migration if still running unsupported SharePoint 2016 or 2019.

  • CVE-2026-56164 is a privilege escalation vulnerability in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server caused by a missing authentication check on a critical function.
  • Microsoft confirmed that CVE-2026-56164 has been exploited in the wild and disclosed it as a zero-day with a CVSS v3.1 base score of 5.3.
  • The vulnerability affects SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, while SharePoint Online is not in scope.
  • Microsoft released patches for CVE-2026-56164 in the July 14, 2026 Patch Tuesday update, but the patch must be applied through SharePoint’s own servicing process rather than only installing a Windows cumulative update.
  • The article recommends inventorying internet-facing SharePoint Server instances, enabling AMSI integration in Full Mode, restricting network access, reviewing logs, and rotating IIS machine keys on farms suspected of compromise.

OkoBot: new sophisticated malware framework targets cryptocurrency users — Should Read

Kaspersky details OkoBot, an active and evolving malware framework delivered via TookPS that targets cryptocurrency users with SSH-based control, hidden browser extensions, keylogging, screen recording, and wallet seed-phrase phishing. The campaign has hit hundreds of victims across more than 25 countries and uses many coordinated modules to steal crypto-related data and credentials.

  • Kaspersky identified OkoBot as an updated TookPS campaign that uses a malware framework with more than 20 payloads and implants to deliver and orchestrate malicious modules via an SSH tunnel.
  • The initial infection is delivered mainly through ClickFix attacks and GitHub-hosted malware masquerading as legitimate software, including a fake SQL Server Management Studio package that was actually Audacity with a malicious implant embedded in one library.
  • After infection, an automated SSH bot collects system information, harvests cryptocurrency wallet files, browser cookies, profiles, and credentials, and sets up Remote Desktop access through a reverse SSH tunnel.
  • OkoBot includes modules such as a hidden browser extension loader, a plugin dispatcher, SeedHunter for Ledger and Trezor seed phrase theft, MC Keylogger, and OkoSpyware for capturing keystrokes and video of targeted application windows.
  • Kaspersky detected hundreds of OkoBot victims in more than 25 countries, with the largest proportions of attacked end users in Brazil, Vietnam, Canada, Mexico, and Türkiye.

Cursor Flaw Lets Malicious Cloned Repositories Trigger Windows Code Execution — Should Read

Cursor on Windows can automatically execute a malicious git.exe placed in a cloned repository’s root when the folder is opened, enabling zero-click code execution as the logged-in user. There is reportedly no patch or advisory yet, so users should treat untrusted repositories as executable content and open them only in isolated environments.

  • Cursor on Windows can execute a file named git.exe from a project root when a repository is opened, with no click, approval dialog, or warning.
  • Mindgard reported the flaw to Cursor on December 15, 2025 and published technical details seven months later, while the article says there was still no patch or Cursor advisory as of July 15.
  • Mindgard’s proof of concept used Windows Calculator renamed to git.exe and committed to the repository root, causing Calculator windows to open automatically while the project remained open.
  • The article says the risk is that a malicious binary in a cloned repository can run as the logged-in user with access to source code, SSH keys, and cloud tokens.
  • Cymulate reported similar Windows executable-search behavior in GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, the Codex desktop app, and Cursor CLI, and said none of those vendors had shipped fixes as of its June 4 write-up.

It Passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. It Was Still a W-2 Heist. — Should Read

A payroll W-2 theft attempt passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because it used a legitimately authenticated consumer ISP mailbox, while the real deception was display-name impersonation and a fresh third-party Reply-To domain. The key lesson is that email authentication verifies the sending domain, not the human identity or legitimacy of the request.

  • A payroll inbox received an urgent request to send the 2025 W-2 PDFs for every employee at every location the same day.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because it was sent from a compromised or attacker-controlled consumer ISP mailbox and routed through the provider’s legitimate mail servers.
  • The email used a display name containing a company leader’s identity while the Reply-To pointed to pointdsk[.]com, a third domain registered roughly two hours before the message was sent.
  • Microsoft scored the message SCL 9, tagged it as high-confidence spam, and placed it in Junk, while IRONSCALES quarantined it outright.
  • The article emphasizes that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validate the sending domain, not the human identity claimed in the display name.

LAPD sidelines relationship with license-plate reader company Flock Safety — Should Read

The LAPD is pausing its use of Flock Safety license-plate reader cameras and not renewing its contract until it can secure enforceable rules on data ownership, privacy, security, and sharing. The move follows an audit finding Flock data led police to investigate 161 people whose cars were wrongly flagged as stolen.

  • The Los Angeles Police Department is not renewing its contract with automated license plate reader company Flock Safety amid a dispute over who controls the data Flock collects.
  • An inspector general’s audit urged the LAPD to stop using Flock technology until enforceable privacy and security rules are added.
  • The audit found that over a two-month period, the LAPD investigated 161 car owners whose vehicles Flock wrongly identified as stolen, according to 404 Media.
  • LAPD Chief Information Officer Dean Gialamas said the department will not use Flock until data, privacy, security, and sharing concerns are resolved through a contract.
  • Flock said the LAPD’s decision was a surprise and that it is working with the department to ensure privacy protections, auditability, accountability, and limits on data access.

New critical infrastructure cybersecurity framework features government, regional council options — May Read

DHS proposed a new public-private critical infrastructure collaboration framework called ANCHOR to replace the eliminated CIPAC system, shifting more cybersecurity resilience work to state and local levels. Health-ISAC warned that without legal protections for sensitive incident sharing, companies may be reluctant to participate candidly.

  • The Department of Homeland Security proposed a new public-private critical infrastructure collaboration system on Tuesday.
  • The proposed system would replace a framework that President Donald Trump eliminated weeks after returning to office.
  • The Trump administration has said it wants to shift more cybersecurity resilience responsibilities to state and local levels.
  • Errol Weiss of Health-ISAC said the government needs to address legal exposures that often prevent companies from sharing information about sensitive cyber incidents.
  • Weiss said industry leaders relied on legal protections in the old CIPAC framework to have candid, strategic conversations about sensitive vulnerabilities.

5 reasons to bring application security data into your exposure management platform — Optional

Tenable argues that integrating application security scanner data into an exposure management platform gives teams code-to-runtime visibility and the context needed to prioritize the riskiest flaws. This helps reduce alert noise, automate remediation, and translate application security risk into business-level exposure metrics.

  • The article argues that application security data often remains isolated in code-scanning tools, making it difficult to correlate code flaws with security issues in cloud workloads, on-prem assets, operational technology systems, identity platforms, and other parts of the environment.
  • The article says integrating application security scanner data into an exposure management platform provides code-to-runtime visibility, including where developers write and deploy code, who owns it, where the code is running, and its blast radius.
  • The article states that exposure management can help prioritize code vulnerabilities by considering context such as whether assets are in production, user identities and entitlements, external accessibility, business criticality, and compliance requirements.
  • The article says integrating agentic application security testing tools with an exposure management platform can help deduplicate code-security findings, investigate issues, assess risk, and orchestrate remediations and patches.
  • The article explains that Tenable One can ingest and normalize static-code security data from tools such as Snyk and other application security testing tools so organizations can manage application security risk alongside other exposure data.

Life Finds a Way: Securing the Enterprise When Everyone Is a Developer — Optional

AI agents are rapidly breaking long-held security assumptions by making everyone a developer, expanding unmanaged attack surfaces, and compressing exploitation timelines from weeks to hours. Security teams need to embrace and secure agentic tools at scale rather than rely on traditional basics or slow adoption cycles.

  • Gadi Evron argues that AI agents are shifting enterprise security from centrally managed IT and shadow IT concerns to an environment where everyone can build infrastructure, workflows, and applications.
  • The discussion highlights that AI has reduced the time from vulnerability discovery to exploitation from weeks or months to hours, making old patching and prioritization assumptions less reliable.
  • Evron says that simply “doing the basics” is no longer sufficient because agents can take unexpected actions and organizations may not even know what those agents have done.
  • Rob Gurzeev and Evron emphasize that security teams now face a scale and coverage problem because many more applications, agents, MCP servers, extensions, and workflows can appear across an organization.
  • Evron recommends that leaders stay hands-on with AI agents, work closely with vendors and startups, and help employees learn to use these tools rather than trying to block adoption.

Firefox, Chrome, Adobe, and VMware Updates Fix Multiple Critical Security Flaws — Optional

Mozilla, Google, Adobe, and Broadcom released security updates fixing multiple critical flaws across Firefox, Chrome, Adobe products, and VMware Avi Load Balancer. Organizations should patch promptly, especially because public exploit code exists for two Firefox vulnerabilities.

  • Mozilla released Firefox 152.0.6 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-15718 and CVE-2026-15719, and said public exploit code exists but it is not aware of attacks in the wild.
  • Google fixed 15 security flaws in Chrome, including two critical use-after-free bugs in Ozone tracked as CVE-2026-15764 and CVE-2026-15765.
  • Adobe published security updates for 88 vulnerabilities, including critical flaws in ColdFusion, Commerce, Experience Manager, and Illustrator.
  • Adobe fixed eight ColdFusion vulnerabilities that could lead to outcomes including arbitrary code execution and privilege escalation in ColdFusion 2025 Update 11 and ColdFusion 2023 Update 22.
  • Broadcom released a fix for CVE-2026-47865, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware Avi Load Balancer that could allow a malicious user with network access to access the Avi Control plane.

SASE Has An AI Blind Spot. Inspecting Packets Is No Longer Enough. — Optional

Traditional SASE architectures that rely on cloud proxy packet inspection struggle to see and control AI and SaaS interactions happening in the browser, especially with modern encryption and certificate pinning. The article argues enforcement must move closer to the endpoint and browser to inspect user intent before data leaves the device.

  • Enterprise workflows now span SaaS applications, browsers, generative AI tools, unsanctioned browser extensions, and autonomous agents, moving many data interactions to the presentation layer where network-centric architectures were not designed to see.
  • Traditional SASE relies on cloud proxies for decryption, inspection, and policy enforcement, but TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, and certificate pinning can prevent this kind of interception and force organizations to create bypass exceptions.
  • The article says these bypass exceptions can shrink the effective security perimeter, while routing sessions through distant cloud inspection paths can add latency and disrupt tools such as video calls.
  • A traditional network proxy may see only a valid encrypted HTTPS connection to an LLM provider and cannot see payload intent, such as an AI agent using model context protocol tool calls to pull proprietary code or internal documentation.
  • The article argues that governing AI and modern SaaS requires enforcement at the browser and endpoint, with traffic dynamically routed to the closest edge infrastructure when network-level security or routing is required.

New Webinar: Closing the Approval Gap in AI-Era Ad Tech — Optional

Reflectiz is promoting an on-demand webinar with Taboola on the “Approval Gap,” where approved marketing tags can silently load unvetted fourth-party scripts with access to sensitive browser-side data. The key takeaway is that security teams need continuous visibility and governance over ad tech scripts because one-time vendor approval no longer reflects what is actually running on their sites.

  • Reflectiz is offering an on-demand webinar with Taboola about the “Approval Gap,” where a previously approved marketing tag may later load third- and fourth-party scripts that security teams have not reviewed.
  • The article says these client-side scripts can have access to forms, checkout fields, and customer data in users’ browsers.
  • Reflectiz co-founder and CEO Idan Cohen and Taboola Director of Product Omri Ariav discuss the issue from both the security-monitoring and ad tech platform perspectives.
  • The article argues that AI-driven ad tech is creating new integrations, endpoints, and data flows faster than point-in-time audits can track.
  • The webinar promises a three-step playbook to inventory, monitor, and govern an organization’s web supply chain without creating operational friction.

item.title: CISA Warns on Exploited SharePoint CVEs as AsyncAPI npm and DriveSurge Campaigns Spread Malware
item.content:encoded:
CISA warns admins to patch actively exploited SharePoint flaws — Must Read

CISA warns that attackers are actively exploiting three on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server flaws to bypass authentication, achieve remote code execution, and steal IIS machine keys for persistence. Admins should urgently apply Microsoft’s latest patches, verify installation, monitor for compromise, and reduce or protect internet exposure.

  • CISA warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, and CVE-2026-56164 to hack internet-exposed on-premises SharePoint Server instances.
  • The three actively exploited vulnerabilities affect all supported self-hosted SharePoint Server versions, including SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.
  • CISA said attackers are using the flaws to bypass authentication, gain remote code execution, steal Internet Information Services machine keys, and gain persistence to deploy malware on compromised systems.
  • Shadowserver tracks nearly 10,000 internet-exposed Microsoft SharePoint servers and more than 800 that are unpatched against CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659.
  • CISA recommended applying Microsoft’s latest patches, verifying successful installation, shortening patching cycles, enabling AMSI integration and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections, and reducing direct internet exposure where possible.

UK Cybercrime Journal: University of Nottingham Breached by ShinyHunters — Must Read

ShinyHunters breached the University of Nottingham and leaked over 40GB of sensitive student, finance, and campus data, including more than 455,000 unique email addresses and highly personal details. The incident is part of a broader campaign targeting education organizations through Oracle PeopleSoft infrastructure using the critical CVE-2026-35273 zero-day.

  • On 9 June 2026, the University of Nottingham was listed as a victim on the ShinyHunters Tor data leak site.
  • ShinyHunters leaked over 40GB of billing and payment records, student finance data, and campus portal exports from the University of Nottingham and its Malaysia and China campuses.
  • Have I Been Pwned analysis found the leaked data contained over 455,000 unique email addresses and personal information including ethnicities, disabilities, and passport numbers.
  • Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group attributed an active compromise and extortion campaign targeting Oracle PeopleSoft infrastructure to UNC6240, also known as ShinyHunters.
  • Google identified over 100 exposed organizations in the Oracle PeopleSoft campaign and noted that 68% were academic institutions, including universities and colleges worldwide.

Compromised AsyncAPI npm Packages Deliver Multi-Stage Botnet Malware — Must Read

Compromised @asyncapi npm packages were used to deliver a multi-stage botnet loader that downloads the Miasma payload from IPFS and can steal credentials, persist, move laterally, and spread through package registries. The attackers abused legitimate GitHub Actions publishing workflows with valid provenance, so affected systems should be treated as potentially compromised if the poisoned modules were loaded.

  • Four compromised npm packages in the @asyncapi namespace were observed distributing a multi-stage botnet loader, affecting @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1, @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, and @asyncapi/specs versions 6.11.2 and 6.11.2-alpha.1.
  • The poisoned packages contained a hidden JavaScript implant that executed when the infected module was loaded by Node.js, not through npm install hooks.
  • The implant downloaded an encrypted second-stage JavaScript loader named sync.js from IPFS, which decoded to the Miasma tasking framework.
  • The Miasma framework supported six command-and-control communication channels: HTTP, Nostr relay, IPFS, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p GossipSub, and an Ethereum smart contract.
  • StepSecurity said the attacker gained push access to repositories and used legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows to publish the packages with valid OIDC provenance attestations, rather than stealing an npm token.

DriveSurge actor uses ClickFix and FakeUpdates to distribute malware via compromised websites — Should Read

The DriveSurge threat actor is compromising websites and using ClickFix social-engineering prompts alongside FakeUpdates lures to deliver malware. The key takeaway is that users should be wary of browser update or fix prompts on websites, as they may be part of an active malware distribution campaign.

  • The article reports that a threat actor named DriveSurge is distributing malware.
  • DriveSurge is using ClickFix as part of the malware distribution activity.
  • DriveSurge is also using FakeUpdates to distribute malware through compromised websites.
  • The malware distribution described in the article involves websites that have been compromised.

US charges alleged operators of Russian bulletproof hosting service — Should Read

U.S. prosecutors charged three Russian nationals accused of running the Media Land and ML.Cloud bulletproof hosting services, which allegedly supported ransomware and cybercrime operations causing over $62 million in damages. The U.S. is also offering up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates or use of the companies.

  • U.S. federal prosecutors unsealed charges against three Russian nationals accused of providing bulletproof hosting services to ransomware gangs that caused over $62 million in damages worldwide.
  • The indictment says Aleksandr Volosovik owned Media Land, Yulia Pankova owned ML Cloud and assisted with legal and financial matters, and Kirill Zatolokin collected customer payments.
  • Media Land and ML.Cloud allegedly provided infrastructure in multiple countries outside Russia, including China, Finland, the Netherlands, and the United States.
  • The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates of the defendants, their malicious cyber activities, or foreign government-linked use of the companies.
  • The United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia previously sanctioned the three defendants and two companies for providing attack infrastructure and technical support to operations including LockBit, Blacksuit, and Play.

Meta, Microsoft, DOJ, and Others Disrupt Southeast Asia Scam Compounds — Should Read

Meta, Microsoft, the U.S. Department of Justice, and partners coordinated actions to disrupt Southeast Asia-based scam compounds that run large-scale online fraud operations. The key takeaway is that major tech platforms and law enforcement are increasingly targeting the infrastructure and accounts enabling these transnational scams.

  • The article reports that Meta, Microsoft, the DOJ, and others disrupted scam compounds.
  • The disrupted scam compounds were located in Southeast Asia.
  • The article identifies Meta, Microsoft, and the DOJ as participants in the disruption effort.

Over 1.4 Million Accounts Disrupted in Cybercrime Crackdown — Should Read

An international cybercrime crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million malicious accounts, highlighting the scale of coordinated efforts to dismantle online fraud and account-abuse infrastructure.

  • The article reports on a cybercrime crackdown.
  • The crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million accounts.
  • The disruption of accounts is presented as the central outcome of the crackdown.

Microsoft: Some Dell PCs shut down after recent Windows updates — May Read

Microsoft is temporarily blocking the KB5101650 Windows 11 security update on some Dell PCs after an Intel driver incompatibility caused shutdowns, overheating, poor performance, and battery drain. A fix is being developed with Dell and is expected soon.

  • Microsoft is blocking the KB5101650 Windows 11 security update on some Dell devices because it can cause shutdowns and performance issues.
  • The issue affects a limited number of Dell systems after installing the KB5101650 cumulative update for Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2 devices.
  • Microsoft said the root cause is a conflict between the new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface introduced in the KB5095093 preview update and the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.
  • Affected devices may show a yellow exclamation point in Device Manager next to the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.
  • Microsoft is working with Dell on a fix and plans to release a resolution for affected devices in the coming days.

ADPathFinder: OpenGraph Attack Path Mapping in BloodHound CE — Optional

NetSPI released ADPathFinder, a tool that uses BloodHound CE graph data to automatically find and group privilege escalation paths across AD, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM. It also enriches password audit results with BloodHound context so cracked or weak credentials can be prioritized by real attack-path risk.

  • ADPathFinder maps privilege escalation paths across Active Directory, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM using BloodHound graph data.
  • The tool combines SharpHound data with OpenGraph collector data from tools such as MSSQLHound and ConfigManBearPig so cross-dataset paths appear as one finding.
  • ADPathFinder groups users and computers that reach the same target through the same chain, reducing duplicate findings in large environments.
  • The tool can run password audits using NTDS dumps and hashcat potfiles, adding BloodHound context such as group membership, roastability, delegation, and account risk.
  • ADPathFinder generates per-domain HTML reports, along with text and JSON outputs, containing severity-organized findings, attack path graphs, and PowerShell commands to confirm each step.

item.title: Microsoft July Patch Tuesday Fixes CVE-2026-56155/56164 as SonicWall SMA1000 Zero-Days Hit
item.content:encoded:
SonicWall warns of SMA1000 flaws exploited in zero-day attacks, patch now — Must Read

SonicWall is urging SMA1000 customers to immediately install hotfixes for two actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities, including a critical SSRF flaw and a post-authentication code injection bug. CISA has added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and SonicWall says compromised appliances should be re-imaged or redeployed with credentials and TOTP tokens reset.

  • SonicWall warned that two SMA1000 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, are being actively exploited in zero-day attacks.
  • CVE-2026-15409 is a critical server-side request forgery vulnerability in the SMA1000 Appliance Work Place interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to force an appliance to make requests to unintended locations.
  • CVE-2026-15410 is a high-severity post-authentication code injection flaw in the SMA1000 Appliance Management Console that could allow a remote authenticated administrator to execute arbitrary operating system commands.
  • The vulnerabilities affect SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v running specified platform-hotfix releases, with fixes available in platform-hotfix versions 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835 and later releases.
  • CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and federal agencies have until July 17, 2026, to secure affected systems or discontinue use of the product if mitigations cannot be applied.

Microsoft Patches Record 622 Flaws, Including Two Zero-Days Under Active Attack — Must Read

Microsoft’s record July Patch Tuesday fixes 622 flaws, including two actively exploited privilege-escalation zero-days in SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services that should be prioritized over higher-scored bugs. Organizations should patch exploited issues first and audit for Kerberos RC4 dependencies before applying updates, as the RC4 rollback option is being removed.

  • Microsoft released its largest Patch Tuesday on record, fixing 622 of its own CVEs according to the Security Update Guide.
  • Two actively exploited zero-days are CVE-2026-56164 in on-premises SharePoint Server and CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services.
  • CVE-2026-56164 lets an unauthenticated attacker escalate privileges over the network, and Microsoft notes that enabling AMSI in Full Mode on the server blunts the attack.
  • CVE-2026-50661 is a publicly disclosed BitLocker bypass that requires physical access to the device and is not reported as under attack.
  • The July update removes the Kerberos RC4 rollback switch, so service accounts that still request RC4 Kerberos tickets may fail authentication after the update.

SAP Patches CVSS 9.9 NetWeaver ABAP Flaw That Could Expose or Modify Data — Must Read

SAP’s July 2026 security updates fix a critical CVSS 9.9 NetWeaver ABAP flaw that could let authenticated attackers corrupt memory to access or modify data or disrupt systems. Customers should apply the patched ABAP Kernel and also address critical Approuter and Commerce Cloud issues involving HTTP smuggling and default OAuth credentials.

  • SAP released July 2026 security updates addressing multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw in SAP NetWeaver Application Server ABAP.
  • CVE-2026-44747 is a CVSS 9.9 out-of-bounds write flaw that can allow an authenticated attacker to cause memory corruption leading to unauthorized data access, data modification, or system unavailability.
  • SAP also fixed CVE-2026-27690, an HTTP request/response smuggling flaw in SAP Approuter deployments in non-Cloud Foundry environments that can expose user responses and trigger denial-of-service attacks.
  • SAP addressed CVE-2026-44761, a default credentials issue in SAP Commerce Cloud involving a sample OAuth 2.0 client with publicly documented sample credentials.
  • The article states there is no evidence that the flaws have been exploited in the wild, but customers are advised to apply the necessary updates.

Microsoft releases Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update — Should Read

Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update with July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes for 570 vulnerabilities, available to Enterprise LTSC and ESU-enrolled devices. The update also fixes several known issues but may break legacy apps using unregistered third-party TDI transports due to new security hardening.

  • Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update, which includes the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates for 570 vulnerabilities and additional security fixes.
  • Consumers enrolled in Microsoft’s free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates program can receive security updates until October 12, 2027, after Microsoft extended the program by an additional year.
  • Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC users and devices enrolled in the ESU program can install KB5099539 through Windows Update by manually checking for updates.
  • After installing KB5099539, Windows 10 is updated to build 19045.7548 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 is updated to build 19044.7548.
  • Microsoft warns that a security hardening change enforcing TDI transport registration requirements may affect legacy applications that rely on unregistered third-party TDI transports.

11 Malicious NuGet Tools Pose as Game Cheats to Drop a Windows Host-Surveillance Payload — Should Read

Socket researchers found 11 malicious NuGet .NET tools posing as game cheats that download and run a Windows payload called pepesoft.exe. The payload collects host and licensing telemetry via Google Sheets, binds activity to hardware IDs, supports remote bans, and in some builds exposes Telegram-controlled screenshot and automation features.

  • Socket’s Threat Research Team analyzed 11 malicious NuGet packages published as .NET command-line tools that pose as game utilities, bots, and panels.
  • Each package acts as a first-stage downloader that retrieves and executes a Windows payload named pepesoft.exe from GitHub Releases and Hugging Face paths under the username pepegit666.
  • The .NET downloaders resolve GitHub download hosts through Google DNS-over-HTTPS, and 10 of the 11 request elevation to resynchronize the Windows system clock before fetching the payload.
  • The recovered pepesoft.exe payloads retrieve remote configuration, authenticate to Google Sheets, bind activations to hardware, and honor a remote hardware-ID and UUID ban list.
  • The direct-bytecode Albion, Calculator, and Throne payloads include Telegram bot commands that can send screenshots back to the configured chat.

US unseals indictment against alleged operators of Russian bulletproof hosting service — Should Read

The U.S. unsealed charges against three Russians accused of running Media Land and ML Cloud, bulletproof hosting services allegedly used by ransomware gangs and stolen-card markets tied to $62 million in victim losses. The State Department is offering up to $10 million for information, including any foreign government links to the operation.

  • Federal prosecutors unsealed an indictment against three Russians associated with the St. Petersburg-based bulletproof hosting provider Media Land and sister company ML Cloud.
  • Aleksandr Volosovik, Yulia Pankova, and Kirill Zatolokin face charges including conspiracy to commit and aid and abet computer fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
  • The indictment cites 44 unnamed victims who suffered $62 million in losses from cybercriminal groups allegedly aided by Media Land and ML Cloud.
  • Authorities said ransomware groups including Lockbit, BlackSuit, and Play, as well as stolen credit card marketplaces including Briansclub and Bidencash, used Media Land or ML Cloud infrastructure.
  • The State Department announced a reward of up to $10 million for information in the case, emphasizing information about foreign government links to Media Land and ML Cloud.

Nearly 300 GitHub repos pose as legit software to push malware — Should Read

A threat actor created nearly 300 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software projects to lure users into downloading a BoryptGrab-like infostealer. The malware steals browser data, crypto wallets, messaging tokens, credentials, and files, then exfiltrates them to a Russia-based command-and-control server.

  • A threat actor published 292 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software and security projects to distribute infostealer malware.
  • Each fake repository included a README file with a download link that sent visitors to a malicious landing page using trust-inspiring wording, branding, and spoofed badges.
  • The downloaded ZIP archive contained a trojanized libcurl.dll and a legitimate signed WinGUP updater that side-loaded the DLL to execute an embedded infostealer in memory.
  • The infostealer appears to be a BoryptGrab variant that steals browser data, cryptocurrency wallet data, messaging and gaming tokens, Windows Credential Manager contents, selected files, screenshots, system details, and installed-software lists.
  • Arctic Wolf reported that GitHub had removed a large portion of the malicious repositories, but several dozen GitHub Pages redirectors still remained active at the time of its report.

Spanish Police take down €140 million cyber fraud ring, arrest four — Should Read

Spanish Police dismantled a cyber fraud and money-laundering network accused of moving about €140 million from investment scams and business email compromise schemes. Four suspects were arrested across Spain, Portugal, and Panama, with €3 million frozen for victims.

  • Spanish Police dismantled a cybercrime and money-laundering organization that made €140 million from investment fraud and business email compromise attacks.
  • Four people were arrested in Spain, Portugal, and Panama as part of the law enforcement operation.
  • Police said the scheme involved at least 800 bank accounts, 120 business accounts, and 67 external accomplices who acted as money mules.
  • Investigators confirmed that €94 million was channeled through the network and linked another €61 million to the group’s 2024 business email compromise operations.
  • Authorities seized 15 computers and more than 170 smartphones, froze €3 million in crime proceeds, and said the main operators had been arrested.

AI Productivity Tools: The Adoption Journey So Far — Optional

AI productivity tools can dramatically increase output, but there is no fixed benchmark for “enough”; the practical goal is continuous improvement. The author argues that success comes from matching the right AI tools to the right tasks, giving clear prompts and goals, and sharing lessons across teams.

  • The author says eight months of serious AI productivity tool use has made him measurably more productive, but he still lacks a clear benchmark for what level of productivity is enough.
  • The author uses different AI tools for different purposes, including ChatGPT for everyday brainstorming and questions, Claude for deeper research and planning, Claude Code and Cursor for coding, and NotebookLM for learning and organizing research.
  • The author built a fully operational internal application for Mitiga’s research team in about five hours using Claude, including conference tracking, submission reviews, dashboards, Slack notifications, SSO, deployment, and security audits.
  • The author says AI has changed his workflow by making it easier to work on three things in parallel because he can refocus on each task instead of rebuilding full context from scratch.
  • The author believes poor AI outputs are usually caused by his own vague prompts, failure to break work into smaller steps, or lack of clarity about the desired end goal.

item.title: Windows 11 Patch Tuesday, ShareFile Zero-Day, LabubaRAT, and Password Manager Phishing
item.content:encoded:
Windows 11 KB5101650 & KB5099414 cumulative updates released — Should Read

Microsoft released mandatory Windows 11 cumulative updates KB5101650 and KB5099414 for versions 25H2/24H2 and 23H2, delivering July 2026 Patch Tuesday security fixes for 571 vulnerabilities. The updates also add minor improvements such as Bluetooth/AirPods pairing fixes, Point-in-Time restore, Widgets and accessibility changes, and File Explorer performance fixes.

  • Microsoft released the mandatory Windows 11 KB5101650 and KB5099414 cumulative updates for versions 25H2/24H2 and 23H2 to fix security vulnerabilities, bugs, and add new features.
  • The updates include the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security patches for 571 vulnerabilities discovered in previous months.
  • After installation, Windows 11 25H2 will move to build 26200.8875, Windows 11 24H2 will move to build 26100.8875, and Windows 11 23H2 will move to build 22631.7376.
  • The update includes Bluetooth-related fixes such as faster AirPods pairing, improved Beats Studio Pro microphone reliability, and more reliable Bluetooth audio connections.
  • Microsoft said it is not aware of any new issues with this month’s Patch Tuesday update.

Progress confirms ShareFile zero-day flaw behind Storage Zone shutdown — Should Read

Progress Software confirmed a high-severity zero-day path traversal flaw in ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers caused last week’s emergency shutdown and has released patches in versions 5.12.5 and 6.0.2. The company says it has no evidence of customer data access or active exploitation but urges customers to update before bringing servers back online.

  • Progress Software confirmed that a high-severity zero-day vulnerability caused the emergency shutdown of ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers last week.
  • The vulnerability is a path traversal flaw affecting all 5.x and 6.x versions of ShareFile Storage Zone Controller.
  • Progress said an authenticated administrative user could read arbitrary files accessible to the application’s service account, write threat actor-controlled content to arbitrary directories, or enumerate the server filesystem layout.
  • Progress released ShareFile Storage Zone Controller versions 5.12.5 and 6.0.2 and urged customers to install the updates before bringing controllers back online.
  • Progress said it currently has no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data and has not identified any active threat.

LabubaRAT Masquerades as NVIDIA Software to Control Windows Hosts — Should Read

Researchers identified LabubaRAT, a previously undocumented Rust-based remote access trojan that disguises itself as NVIDIA software while giving attackers control over Windows hosts. It supports host profiling, command execution, file transfer, screenshots, SOCKS5 proxying, and multiple C2 channels including HTTPS, WebView2, and DNS tunneling.

  • Blackpoint Cyber researchers reported a previously undocumented Rust-based remote access trojan called LabubaRAT that masquerades as NVIDIA software on Windows hosts.
  • LabubaRAT supports HTTPS, WebView2, and DNS tunneling for communication, allowing attackers to maintain access if one communication path is detected and closed.
  • The attack chain begins with an executable named nvidia-sysruntime.exe, which impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit and accepts command-and-control configuration through command-line arguments.
  • LabubaRAT stores its configuration in a local SQLite database and inventories browsers, security products, hostname, RAM size, CPU model, and Windows User Account Control state.
  • The malware can execute commands, run PowerShell and JavaScript, capture screenshots, upload and download files, handle archives, and provide SOCKS5 proxy support.

LastPass, Bitwarden users targeted with fake security alerts — Should Read

LastPass and Bitwarden users are being targeted by phishing emails that impersonate security policy updates and lead to fake DocuSign-style sites on lookalike domains. Users should avoid clicking these messages, never enter master passwords on linked sites, and change credentials immediately if they interacted with the phishing pages.

  • LastPass is warning users about a phishing campaign that uses fake security notices to direct recipients to fraudulent websites.
  • The phishing emails sent from hello@lastpassnewsletter.com claim there are LastPass service policy changes and lead users to a fake DocuSign-style page on lastpasscompliance[.]com.
  • LastPass says its systems have not been compromised and that the phishing emails did not originate from its infrastructure.
  • BleepingComputer found that Bitwarden users are targeted by similar emails sent from hello@bitwardennewsletter.com and redirected to bitwardencompliance[.]com.
  • LastPass advises users who entered credentials on phishing sites to change their master passwords immediately from a trusted device and review their vaults for suspicious activity.

Finland issues wanted notice for hacker behind massive psychotherapy data breach — May Read

Finnish police have issued a wanted notice for convicted Vastaamo hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki after the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal, making his nearly seven-year sentence final. Authorities are seeking to return him to prison for the massive psychotherapy data breach and extortion of thousands of patients.

  • Finnish police issued a wanted notice for convicted hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki after Finland’s Supreme Court refused to hear his appeal.
  • The Supreme Court’s decision leaves in place a February Court of Appeal ruling sentencing Kivimäki to nearly seven years in prison for hacking psychotherapy provider Vastaamo and extorting both the company and its patients.
  • Eastern Uusimaa Police said officers have been instructed to arrest Kivimäki if he is located and transfer him to Vantaa Prison to serve the rest of his sentence.
  • Kivimäki has denied carrying out the attack and argued that prosecutors relied largely on circumstantial evidence and disputed digital and cryptocurrency evidence.
  • The Vastaamo breach exposed information on about 33,000 patients, and more than 24,000 people reported receiving extortion demands.

Frontier AI in the Health Sector: Managing Supply Chain and Vendor Risk — Optional

Frontier AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, forcing healthcare organizations to shrink remediation timelines from weeks to days or hours. The paper urges healthcare entities to update vendor contracts, improve third-party visibility, and build contingency plans to manage AI-driven supply chain risk.

  • Frontier AI models can identify vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed, creating new risks for systems and data in the health sector.
  • The article says health sector organizations must move vulnerability remediation from multi-week timelines to days or hours, with patching and patch validation prioritized.
  • The paper focuses on how health sector organizations should work with supply chains and third-party partners as frontier AI changes the threat model.
  • The article recommends revisiting supplier contracts to require faster remediation windows and greater visibility into vendor security practices.
  • The article says organizations should maintain a complete inventory of third-party software, develop contingency strategies, map external digital assets, adopt zero-trust principles, and communicate transparently with supply chain partners.

AI Agents Are Creating a New Class of Employee Risk — Optional

AI agents are becoming a new source of enterprise security risk because they can autonomously access sensitive data and take damaging actions at machine speed. Organizations need data-centric controls that evaluate actions and intent, not just access permissions, to adopt AI safely.

  • AI agents are creating a new digital workforce that rapidly increases the number of non-human identities accessing sensitive data.
  • The article cites PocketOS as an example where Cursor deleted the business, including the database and all backups, while performing a routine task.
  • AI agents can act autonomously on enterprise data and take actions at machine speed and scale, which can make small mistakes or misconfigurations have large impacts.
  • The article says model safeguards alone are not enough because AI agents do not inherently understand risk or policy.
  • Organizations need data-level controls that connect data sensitivity, permissions, identity, and activity to determine whether an action should be allowed.

You Don't Have to Run an Exploit to Know If You're Vulnerable — Optional

The article argues that security teams can no longer rely on patching every new CVE fast enough and should instead validate which flaws are actually exploitable in their own environments. It promotes Picus’s approach of testing attacker behavior chains safely, without firing real exploits, to prioritize the exposures that matter most.

  • The article says the first half of 2026 produced more CVEs than any full year on record before 2024, at a rate of about one new CVE every 7.4 minutes.
  • The article says AI has reduced the time between a public advisory and a working exploit, with the Zero Day Clock putting the 2026 median time-to-exploit at well under a day.
  • The article argues that live exploit testing is limited because it can only be used where it is safe and where a usable exploit already exists, which the article says covers only 10 to 15% of most enterprise attack surfaces.
  • The article describes Picus Platform’s TTP-chaining approach as testing the required steps of an exploit against deployed defenses to determine whether the full attack chain would succeed without firing the real exploit.
  • The article uses Nightmare-Eclipse as an example, describing BlueHammer, RedSun, and UnDefend as Windows zero-day releases that can be modeled through safe actions such as creating a test service, accessing registry hives through Volume Shadow Copy, and stopping Windows Defender.

10 Black Hat NOCs and Counting: Corelight Sees It All | Corelight — Optional

Corelight highlights its decade-long role supporting the Black Hat network operations center, emphasizing how its network visibility helps detect, investigate, and understand activity on one of the world’s most challenging conference networks.

  • The article is titled “10 Black Hat NOCs and Counting: Corelight Sees It All.”
  • The article identifies Corelight as the organization associated with the piece.
  • The title states that Corelight has been involved with 10 Black Hat NOCs and counting.

item.title: Microsoft Entra MFA Changes, Phishing Kits, OAuth Spoofing, and SAP Critical Flaws
item.content:encoded:
OAuth Client ID Spoofing Lets Attackers Validate Stolen Microsoft Entra Credentials — Must Read

Proofpoint says threat actors are abusing OAuth client ID spoofing in Microsoft Entra ID to enumerate accounts and validate stolen passwords without generating normal successful sign-in telemetry. The technique fragments attempts across fake application IDs, helping campaigns targeting millions of users evade application-based detections, rate limits, and some Conditional Access policies.

  • Proofpoint said at least two threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns to enumerate Microsoft Entra ID user accounts and validate stolen credentials without generating successful sign-in events.
  • The technique uses spoofed client IDs in HTTP POST requests to Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 token endpoint with the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow, allowing attackers to infer account and password validity from AADSTS error responses.
  • When a spoofed client ID is used, Entra sign-in logs record only the application ID without a corresponding application name, which can cause detections based on specific application names to miss the activity.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_pyreq2323 as targeting more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants from AWS infrastructure between January and March 2026, causing lockouts for roughly 28% of targeted users.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_OutFlareAZ as starting in December 2025 and using Cloudflare infrastructure to target over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

SAP warns of critical flaws in NetWeaver and Commerce Cloud — Must Read

SAP’s July 2026 security updates fix 16 vulnerabilities, including three critical flaws in NetWeaver AS ABAP, SAP Approuter, and SAP Commerce Cloud that could enable data access, modification, denial of service, or abuse of default credentials. SAP says it has not seen evidence of exploitation yet, but customers should patch promptly.

  • SAP addressed 16 vulnerabilities across multiple products in its July 2026 security updates, including three critical flaws in NetWeaver, Commerce Cloud, and AppRouter.

  • The article groups malicious Python package techniques into build hook abuses, such as setup.py command classes, .pth files, site hook modules, and PYTHONPATH manipulation, and package content abuses, such as import-time payloads, __main__.py scripts, entry point hijacking, and overriding legitimate package contents.
  • Persistent techniques described in the article include .pth files and sitecustomize or usercustomize hooks, which can run payloads every time Python is invoked in the affected environment.
  • Recommended defenses include scanning packages with tools such as pip-audit, using lock files and cryptographic hashes, installing packages in isolated environments, applying dependency cooldowns, generating SBOMs, and using PyPI Trusted Publishing.
